title: "This is Catastrophic": Gaza Hit Hard by UN Food Cuts and Lack of Humanitarian Aid
author: Abdel Qader Sabbah

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fddd35b36-c6ae-4748-9d91-87744392f6f5_3020x1696.png)Al-
Abd Abu Beid prepares a meal of lentils from food rations distributed by the
World Food Programme, one day after the UN agency announced it would reduce
food aid in Gaza by around one-third. October 20, 2026. Screenshot from
footage by Abdel Qader Sabbah.

GAZA CITY--Al-Abd Abu Beid set a box of food rations down on a pile of stones
he uses as a makeshift table outside his ramshackle tent on the coastline west
of Gaza City. The cardboard box displayed the blue logo of the United Nations
World Food Programme (WFP), along with a stamp showing it had been packed on
July 11, 2026. Abu Beid sifted through the contents: a plastic bottle of
sunflower oil, a bag of red split lentils, and eight cans of hummus or white
beans.

"We have no income at all," Abu Beid told Drop Site News. "We depend heavily
on the brown boxes from the World Food Programme."

"We were actually hoping they would improve the contents of these boxes,
because they contain rice, lentils, and the same things over and over again,"
he continued. "Instead, we were shocked to hear that they're going to cut it
off."

Abu Beid spoke to Drop Site on October 20--one day after the WFP
[announced](https://www.wfp.org/news/funding-cuts-force-wfp-drastically-
reduce-lifesaving-assistance-gaza) it was reducing food aid in Gaza by around
one-third, cutting off access to half a million Palestinians from critical
food assistance due to funding shortages. The cuts also reduce food rations by
half--with families receiving only one food parcel a month instead of two--and
a smaller bag of wheat flour. In addition, WFP cut the number of daily hot
meals it provides from 250,000 to 150,000. Meanwhile, families living in the
most hard-to-reach areas of Gaza, including near the yellow line of Israeli
military control, will now receive a hot meal every other day instead of
daily. The value of cash assistance provided to 75,000 families would also be
reduced, the UN agency said.

"What is a family supposed to do? I have seven people in my family. How am I
supposed to feed them? Even if the food was repetitive, just rice and lentils,
I have no income, so I relied on it to cook for my children," Abu Beid said.
"This is a humanitarian crime. People are being killed and slaughtered every
day, and now you're cutting off their food too. This is catastrophic."

The WFP announcement came a little over a year after the "ceasefire" agreement
that was supposed to bring an end to Israel's assault on Gaza and restore the
delivery of food, fuel, medicine, and other life essentials to what experts
say are the minimum required levels.

Instead, the Israeli military has continued its attacks, killing over 1,500
men, women and children while severely restricting the amount of aid allowed
into Gaza in violation of the agreement. In October alone, Israel killed 143
Palestinians in direct attacks, according to the Health Ministry, including 23
children, and injured over 670.

The unrelenting Israeli assault prompted a UN Independent International
Commission of Inquiry to [conclude](https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-
releases/2026/10/israel-has-committed-war-crimes-and-crimes-against-humanity-
occupied) earlier this month that Israel is continuing to "commit genocidal
acts even after the so-called ceasefire agreement, with the intent to destroy
the Palestinian people, in whole or in part."

With the genocide now its fourth year, levels of hunger and malnutrition are
once again growing. In the same announcement that it was heavily reducing food
assistance to Gaza, the WFP said that an estimated 1.4 million Palestinians,
or 67% of Gaza's population, are experiencing acute food insecurity at "crisis
levels or worse." Some 200,000 people remain in "emergency conditions," where
immediate food assistance is needed to prevent deaths from hunger.

###### Video: Families in a tent encampment on the shoreline west of Gaza
prepare meager meals with UN food rations and people gather in Al-Shati
refugee camp to protest against UN aid cuts. October 20, 2026. Footage by
Abdel Qader Sabbah.

"We depend on these parcels for everything: flour, rice, lentils, paste,
chickpeas, and beans. Most of what we eat is beans, rice, and lentils. We use
the flour to make bread on a metal griddle over a fire," Linda Abu Warda told
Drop Site. She sat stirring a blackened pot filled with a rice stew as her
husband, Fares, fed small pieces of wood into the fire beneath it--a thin
metal box serving as a makeshift stove. "Now they're saying the aid has
stopped, or that it's going to stop. We're already barely managing to get by
with what little we have. Imagine what will happen if they cut it off
completely. I have children, as you can see. They'll die of hunger."

She added, "We've already lived through famine. We've experienced it. We were
hoping they'd increase the amount of aid we receive, not reduce it."

In mid-2025, Gaza was plunged into a full-blown famine, with Palestinians
collapsing in the streets and men, women, and children dying from hunger and
malnutrition on a daily basis. An Israeli starvation campaign that included a
full blockade in March 2025 was followed by a privatized "aid distribution"
system overseen by the U.S. and Israeli-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation
(GHF) that replaced the UN. With just four distribution sites across the
entirety of the enclave, guarded by American mercenaries and located in areas
occupied by Israeli soldiers, the GHF sites became death traps for starving
Palestinians seeking food. More than 2,600 Palestinians were killed at or near
GHF distribution sites or at the few UN convoys allowed inside.

"We hope they'll allow this aid to enter officially and legally, instead of
forcing us to go back to Zikim like before, when people had to risk their
lives just to bring home a bite of food for their children," Linda's husband,
Fares, said, referring to one of the aid distribution sites in 2025 where
hundreds of Palestinians were killed. "A man would go out and instead of
coming home with a bag of flour, he'd come back in a body bag."

Food prices have soared as a result of food shortages and arbitrary closures
of the crossings into Gaza by Israel. In mid-October, Israel suddenly halted
all commercial shipments into Gaza. While commercial goods were eventually
allowed back in after several days, the brief closure nevertheless sent prices
shooting upward.

"The closure of the crossings is what's driving prices up," Linda Abu Warda
said. "When we want to cook a meal, we can't even afford a single onion, it's
expensive. Onions cost 30 or 40 shekels a kilo [about $9.5 to $12.75], so
we've had to do without them…They used to cost four or five shekels [about
$1.25 to $1.60]." She added, "People don't have the money to buy anything.
They've raised the prices of sugar, food, cooking oil, and vegetables."

Other humanitarian groups have also reduced aid distribution to Gaza. In May,
World Central Kitchen (WCK), the biggest provider of hot meals in Gaza
[announced](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/gaza-world-central-kitchen-food-
hunger-israel-blockade) it was cutting its distribution in half, from around
one million meals a day to 500,000. WCK said the decision was "driven entirely
by financial pressure," citing rising food prices as a result of the
U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

"The famine has not ended in Gaza," Ahmed Abu Qamar, a writer and economic
affairs researcher in Gaza City, told Drop Site. "Perhaps its severity has
eased slightly. When we look back at last summer, the famine was extremely
severe. Since the ceasefire agreement last October, Israel has been pursuing a
policy of engineered starvation. In other words, it may allow people the bare
minimum to eat each day, or even less than that, but it does not provide them
with what they need to achieve food security and sustain their lives."

## "We're extremely, extremely afraid of winter"

Mohammed Zayed, who lives in the same tent encampment on the sandy shoreline
west of Gaza City, used rudimentary tools to try and erect a wall of tarp and
blankets around his tent. Wind billowed through the pieces of cloth and tarp
hanging from thin metal poles and pieces of wood hammered into the ground and
connected by lengths of wire and rope.

"Here on the beach, we suffer terribly in both summer and winter. And now, as
winter approaches, we're trying to prepare because living here is extremely
difficult," Zayed told Drop Site on October 14. "These tents can't withstand
that because they're worn out and falling apart. They're three years old now.
"

"We're extremely, extremely afraid of winter," he continued. "We try to stitch
up tarps and secure the metal poles properly. We're trying to reduce the
impact of the wind, because otherwise it'll blow everything away. It's
extremely difficult for me and for everyone here. People's tents are worn out,
falling apart, collapsing around them. Nobody has the means to replace a tent
or change the tarps to prepare for winter."

"All of this is just an illusion," he said, pointing to the tarps. "All of
this will be blown away."

Zayed's tent is part of a vast tent encampment on the northern Gaza coastline.
Nearly the entirety of Gaza's population has been forced to displace by
Israel's assault, with many families displaced multiple times. The majority of
Palestinians in Gaza are now living crammed in tent encampments. Dilapidated
tents now occupy every open space, with streets, squares, stadiums,
courtyards, and fields filled with tent encampments.

###### Video: Families in a tent encampment west of Gaza City try to prepare
their tents for winter with few supplies. In the Jabaliya refugee
camp,Mohammed Al-Shabrawi tries to cover up the broken walls of his badly
damaged home. October 14, 2026. Footage by Abdel Qader Sabbah.

The lack of proper shelter has been disastrous and even fatal, particularly in
winter with torrential rains, high winds, flooding, and cold temperatures.
Over the past three winters, Palestinians--mostly infants--[have
died](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/winter-cold-collapsing-buildings-
palestinians-killed-israeli-blockade) of hypothermia in Gaza as a result of
exposure, including [11 children](https://www.unicef.org/sop/reports/unicef-
state-palestine-humanitarian-situation-update) last winter alone.

"The humanitarian situation remains catastrophic with the near totality of the
population still surviving in deteriorated tents and makeshift shelters,
bracing for a fourth winter without adequate protection from the cold, wind,
rain and flooding risks," the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian
Affairs noted in its latest situation
[report](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-
report-22-october-2026) last week.

Since the ceasefire, Israel has continued to push inward, expanding the yellow
line that demarcates its area of control, driving Palestinians further west
onto just 30% of the enclave. Israel has also blocked the entry of
reconstruction materials, mobile homes, and heavily restricted the number of
tents and shelter materials allowed into Gaza in violation of the agreement.

"Those displaced before the announcement of a ceasefire have little to no
prospect of return to the areas they fled, most of which are inaccessible
because they fall beyond the so-called yellow line. And they continue to be
displaced again and again," said Ajith Sunghay, the head of UN Human Rights in
the occupied territories, in a
[statement](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-
territory/displacement-deepens-israeli-forces-push-palestinians-shrinking-
space-enar) last week. "There must be an end to this suffering. This is the
fourth year of displacement for most Palestinians in Gaza, the fourth winter
in tents too flimsy to withstand the rain, and they are still under fire
through it all."

Before the genocide, Khalda Ghattas lived in an apartment in the Tuffah
neighborhood of Gaza City. "I used to live in an apartment building protected
by concrete, with warmth, mattresses, furniture sets, and carpets. What a
beautiful home it was," she told Drop Site. Now, she lives in a flimsy tent on
the sand. "Then we were displaced to the port. The cold is already eating us
alive. We can't keep the wind out."

She continued, "You put up a tarp, another one falls down. You put up a
blanket, it falls too. And the biggest problem is that I can't afford to buy
good, sturdy tarps. And even if I bought one, I'd need metal poles to hold it
up. We have nothing." Due to the severe shortages, Ghattas said a tarp can
cost between 180 and 200 shekels (around $57 to $64). "Where am I supposed to
get that money? I simply can't afford it," she said. "We're still in autumn,
but we already can't withstand the wind. And I have children, as you can see.
I have so many children, including babies. This little girl has asthma, and I
have children with respiratory diseases. I suffer from rheumatism, and my
husband has a heart condition."

Nasser Al-Shanbari, who was displaced from Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza, now
runs a small street stall in Gaza City selling tarps, mattresses, sheets and
other shelter items.

"Tarps have become scarcer this season, prices have gone up, and people have
very little money," Al-Shanbari told Drop Site. "Some of the tarps we have
aren't even any good. The ones we get these days don't last more than two or
three months in the wind and rain before they fall apart. Prices have risen,
and deliveries have also decreased recently. We buy them from people and from
traders, but the quantities available are very limited."

He continued, "A plank that used to cost 10 shekels now costs 150 shekels. A
small measure of nails that used to cost 10 shekels now costs 50. All of this
is expensive. To fix up a shelter with wood, nails, and tarps, it would cost
at least around 5,000 shekels [about $1,600]."

With little recourse, many families have taken to seeking shelter in badly
damaged buildings that are at risk of collapse. In one of the deadliest cases,
at least 21 Palestinians, including 12 children, were killed and 45 others
injured when a residential building collapsed in Gaza City in September. More
than 100 people were estimated to have been sheltering in the building.

Mohammed Al-Shabrawi is currently living in his badly damaged family home in
the Jabaliya refugee camp close to the yellow line. Like nearly every building
in the area, his home was bombed during the war, killing several members of
his family. Barely any of the walls remain intact, with many rooms exposed to
the elements. Al-Shabrawi has taken to affixing tarps and sheets to try and
shield himself from the elements.

"We're trying to seal off the openings with tarps and strips of fabric. Even
the wall behind me is made of tarp, and everything you see here is covered
with tarps. It's extremely difficult for us to buy them because they're so
expensive," Al-Shabrawi told Drop Site.

"We're living in a bombed out house… We're struggling to cover the walls and
roof. When it rains tomorrow, the entire roof will leak. There isn't a single
part of it that doesn't leak and let water pour down on us."

_Sharif Abdel Kouddous and Jawa Ahmad contributed to this report. Sami
Vanderlip edited the video._
